record.title: SciExam reports AI agent systems building ENSO models that beat a published benchmark reference
record.summary: A new arXiv benchmark asks AI agent systems to build compact stochastic models of El Niño–Southern Oscillation from observations. The paper reports that six of twelve final agent submissions scored above its published reference overall and that some agent-built models better matched reconstruction or held-out forecast measures, while the reference led on statistical matching. The paper's two model families echo competing explanations of ENSO asymmetry, but do not resolve the physical debate. Results come from one six-hour run per system, with limited single-run access controls; independent reproduction is open.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors introduce SciExam for ENSO, a six-hour task in which agent systems construct low-order stochastic ENSO models from observations, freeze diagnostics, and are scored on statistics, hidden-variable reconstruction and forecasts over held-out years.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In the paper's final submissions, six of twelve agent systems score above the published reference overall (0.378); the authors report 0.515 for Fable 5.1, 0.479 for Kimi K3 and 0.443 for GPT-5.6 Sol. Systems are evaluated as model–harness submissions, not isolated model weights.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports metric tradeoffs: the published reference performs best on statistical matching, while several agent submissions score better on reconstruction or forecasting. The strongest agent-built models fall into two families corresponding to nonlinear-drift and multiplicative-stochastic-forcing explanations of ENSO asymmetry.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that one controlled-access run of the top system under varied data access found that web access could distract from the task observations; the paper also reports that literature access shifted a model toward sparser theory-based couplings. Each controlled condition used a single run.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The benchmark does not establish repeatable agent capability, a causal effect of data access, or which physical explanation of ENSO asymmetry is correct; independent replication and repeated submissions remain open.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent rerun of the benchmark or verification of its code, data and scoring pipeline was conducted.
Agent systems and the published reference had different observation access, while each system's headline score is based on a single final run.
The candidate ENSO mechanism families are generated and judged within this benchmark and do not establish which physical explanation is correct.

brief.importance_rationale: If reproducible, agent construction of compact climate models that match diagnostics and forecast held-out periods could materially change programs for evaluating scientific reasoning and model discovery. The paper reports a bounded, one-off benchmark and does not establish new ENSO physics or repeatable agent capability.
limitations: The headline is based on twelve final one-off agent-system submissions, not repeated trials; one run per system cannot establish variance or repeatability.
The published reference had observations covering all three periods, while agent systems used 35 years and were evaluated on a never-seen 2015–2024 period; comparison conditions differ.
The benchmark combines model, scaffold and tool choices, so scores cannot be attributed to model weights alone.
The paper's controlled-access ablations use one run per condition and do not establish causal effects of web or literature access.
Two families of fitted low-order models reflect candidate explanations of ENSO asymmetry; their appearance in this benchmark does not resolve the physical mechanism or establish new climate science.
The benchmark selects and scores simplified models using its own diagnostics; broader scientific validity beyond those diagnostics is not established.
brief.summary: A new arXiv benchmark asks AI agent systems to build compact stochastic models of El Niño–Southern Oscillation from observations. The paper reports that six of twelve final agent submissions scored above its published reference overall and that some agent-built models better matched reconstruction or held-out forecast measures, while the reference led on statistical matching. The paper's two model families echo competing explanations of ENSO asymmetry, but do not resolve the physical debate. Results come from one six-hour run per system, with limited single-run access controls; independent reproduction is open.

technical.claimed_result: Six of twelve final agent-system submissions scored above the published reference overall in the authors' SciExam task; measures of statistical fit, hidden-variable reconstruction and held-out forecasting did not rank systems identically.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper specifies a six-hour task budget per agent system; this is a benchmark budget, not a reported measure of inference cost or economic efficiency.
technical.demonstrated_result: Direct inspection confirms that arXiv v1 describes the task and reports these author-run results. This activation did not run the benchmark or independently reproduce them.
technical.implementation_status: The paper reports released code and data availability at lines 338–342; this activation inspected the HTML paper but did not retrieve or execute those artifacts.
technical.mechanism: Agents receive observational data and a six-hour budget to build low-order stochastic ENSO models, freeze diagnostic code and submit outputs. Hidden scoring evaluates statistical properties, reconstruction of hidden variables and forecasts on held-out years.
technical.regime: Twelve final agent-system submissions are compared with a published reference. Agents use 35 years of observations and are evaluated on a never-seen 2015–2024 period; the paper says the reference used observations spanning all three periods. Systems combine models and harnesses, so rankings are not model-only comparisons.
technical.reproducibility: The headline results are twelve final one-off submissions. Access-control comparisons for the top system are also single runs, and the benchmark has not been independently reproduced in this activation.
technical.strongest_baseline: The published reference scores 0.378 overall. Six of twelve final agent submissions exceed it; the paper reports Fable 5.1 at 0.515, Kimi K3 at 0.479 and GPT-5.6 Sol at 0.443. The reference is strongest on statistical matching, while agent entries often do better on reconstruction or forecasting.

brief.title: SciExam reports AI agent systems building ENSO models that beat a published benchmark reference
brief.why_it_matters: This is a concrete test of whether agent systems can construct compact scientific models against hidden diagnostics and held-out observations, beyond answering a fixed question. If replicated, it could inform how research agents are evaluated for model building. The reported scores are one-off benchmark outcomes, and the candidate mechanism families are not confirmed discoveries about ENSO.
